Compatible jets on closed sets

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), September 2026. Public domain (CC0).

*Exposition on prerequisites and compact components by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0. *

Prescribing a function and its derivatives on a closed set is more than assigning numbers at its points. Nearby assignments must fit one Taylor expansion to the required order. Whitney's extension theorem says that this compatibility is exactly what is needed. The proof glues local Taylor polynomials at a scale comparable to the distance from the set. Its estimate then describes what a finite-order distribution supported on that set can measure.

The preceding jet lesson proves smooth mollification, indicator cutoffs, pairings with compactly supported distributions on all suitable smooth functions, and the vanishing-jet theorem. The complete integral Taylor proof supplies every Taylor remainder used here. The kernel lesson supplies support localization and smooth test-space topology. The supplied scalar foundation, §§12–13, proves Euclidean compactness, finite-coordinate calculus, cutoffs and uniform limits; the measure foundation, §§15.0–15.1, provides cube volumes, integration and changes of variables. We prove the full finite-order extension construction, its partition and norm bound below. The references give the finite-jet extension theorem and its distributional applications.

Infinitely many components defeat every finite jet bound

The preceding paired-point example illustrates a general obstruction. It applies to every compact set with infinitely many connected components, including sets whose individual components are intervals or higher-dimensional bodies.

A subset of is relatively clopen if it is both open and closed in the relative topology of .

Lemma 5.1 (separating compact components). In a compact subset , two points in different connected components can be separated by a relatively clopen subset of . If has infinitely many components, there are pairwise disjoint nonempty relatively clopen compact sets , points , and such that

Proof. The component containing a point exists: take the union of all connected subsets containing . This union is connected, because a separation would separate one of those subsets, all of which meet at . It is maximal by the same union argument. The closure of a connected set is connected: each nonempty relatively open part of a separation of the closure meets the dense original set. Consequently components are closed, and components of a compact set are compact.

Let be the intersection of all relatively clopen subsets of containing . It is compact and contains the component of : a connected subset containing cannot meet both sides of a clopen separation. We show that is connected. Otherwise write as a separation into disjoint nonempty compact sets, with . Their distance is positive: a minimum is attained on , and a zero minimum would be a common point. Choose disjoint open neighborhoods in containing , respectively.

For each , some relatively clopen set contains but excludes , by the definition of . The sets cover that compact complement. A finite subcover gives a relatively clopen intersection with If the complement is empty, take . The set is relatively clopen in : inside its complement is , and itself is relatively clopen. It contains , so the definition of forces , contradicting . Thus is the component of . A point outside it is excluded by one of the clopen sets in the defining intersection. This proves the first assertion.

Start with . Whenever the relatively clopen compact set has infinitely many components, choose points in two different components and separate them by the first assertion, applied within . Both resulting pieces are nonempty and relatively clopen in . At least one has infinitely many components; keep such a piece as and call the other . To justify the component count, a connected subset of cannot cross this clopen separation, so its components are exactly the components of the two pieces. This also shows that each inductive use has the required hypothesis.

The discarded are nonempty compact sets and are pairwise disjoint. Choose one point in each. Compactness supplies a convergent subsequence, with limit . For any fixed , all sufficiently late points of this sequence lie outside . Its relatively open property therefore implies . Pass to a further subsequence with distances at most , and relabel its sets and points. They still have all the stated clopen and disjointness properties, and their distances to are positive. This proves (C1).

Corollary 5.3 (a necessary topological condition). Suppose every distribution supported in a compact admits a bound of the form (C3), with and allowed to depend on the distribution. Then has finitely many connected components.

Proof. If it had infinitely many, Theorem 5.2 would give one distribution for which no choice of works.

For a compact set, having finitely many components is equivalent to being a finite union of compact connected sets. One direction uses the compactness of components proved in Lemma 5.1; for the other, each connected member of such a finite cover lies within one component, so the cover can meet only finitely many components. Finiteness alone is a necessary condition here; no converse without a geometric hypothesis is asserted.

On the real line, set

The intervals are disjoint, since the upper endpoint of is less than the lower endpoint of . Each is relatively clopen in . The only possible limit point obtained by visiting infinitely many intervals is zero, so is closed and bounded, hence compact. Intervals are connected by the intermediate value theorem. Each is therefore a component; the remaining component is , because a connected subset containing zero cannot cross any of the clopen separations.

Exercise 1 (basic: the order-zero condition). Show that consists of all continuous functions on . Prove that its norm is equivalent to the supremum norm, and explain how Theorem 3.1 supplies a bounded linear compactly supported continuous extension.

Exercise 2 (intermediate: reproducing a polynomial). On the interval , prescribe , , . Verify compatibility for , compute the normalized remainders, and determine the extension before the final cutoff in (3.5). What remains true after that cutoff?

Exercise 3 (intermediate: incompatible assignments). On , prescribe and . Show that both assigned functions are continuous on , but that the jet is not compatible for . Prove directly that no extension could have those traces.

Exercise 4 (advanced: finite and infinite closed supports). Prove that, on a fixed finite set , the norm (1.4) is bounded by a constant times the first jet-value sum alone. Deduce the corresponding bound for every order-at-most- distribution supported in . Compare this with (4.2) and identify the geometric quantity that ceases to be bounded uniformly.

Exercise 5 (advanced: completeness and a projection). Prove that is complete for (1.4). Let denote the functions with bounded continuous derivatives through order , with their global derivative supremum norm. Show that jet restriction is bounded, and that is a bounded projection on , whose kernel consists exactly of functions with all these jets zero on .

Exercise 6 (intermediate: convergence with cancellation). In (C4), put . Prove convergence to uniformly on every family of smooth functions with uniformly bounded first derivatives on . Give an explicit tail bound using (C1). Explain why neither unpaired positive series defines the same limit.

Exercise 7 (intermediate: interval components). For (C7), compute for every positive integer , using the smooth-function pairing of the compact distribution. Compute , and prove that this distribution is neither zero nor positive. Reconcile these facts with the positive coefficients of each in its finite partial sums.

Exercise 8 (advanced: the role of the infinitely many components). Let be a finite union of pairwise disjoint compact convex sets. Prove directly, using the extension estimate (4.1), that every order-at-most- distribution supported in is bounded by derivatives through order on . Identify which constant in your proof is unavailable for the infinitely many intervals (C7).

Exercise 9 (intermediate: why every functional matters). On the space of finite scalar sequences, put and . Show that every coordinate functional is bounded for , but that the -bounded functional is not. Explain why checking only coordinate functionals would not justify Theorem 6.1.
